name_en: Ruby 18 Black (Hong Yu, Sun Moon Lake)
cultivar: Hong Yu (TTES #18): a Burmese large-leaf Assam line crossed with Taiwan's native wild mountain tea
processing: Fully oxidised orthodox black: bud-and-two-leaf shoots withered long, rolled into long twisted strips, oxidised and dried; no cutting and no roast.
harvest_season: Picked several times a year; summer (June–August) is the prized season for black tea here, with the strongest mint-cinnamon aroma, autumn next, and spring lots are lighter.
appearance_dry: Long, wiry, twisted black strips, often three or four centimetres, glossy with a few golden tips.
appearance_wet: Large, whole, coppery-red leaves, soft and even.
taste_profile: A signature cooling note of mint and cinnamon over a sweet, malty body with dark honey and a hint of camphor; smooth, with little astringency when brewed sensibly.

brewing.notes: Use a pot roomy enough for the long leaf. Western-style: 3 g per 250 ml at 90–95 °C for three minutes; boiling water and long steeps bring out tannin it does not need. Superb cold-brewed.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year and season, with summer-harvest lots the most prized and spring the lightest; the Yuchi Farmers' Association grades lots in its Sun Moon Lake black tea competition and the area has a certified-origin label worth looking for, since cheaper TTES #8 is sometimes sold simply as 'Sun Moon Lake black'. It keeps two or three years sealed and some drinkers prefer it after a year's rest; it is not an ageing tea.
description:
Ruby 18, or Hong Yu, 'red jade', is Taiwan's flagship black tea and the reason Sun Moon Lake is on tea maps again. It is a cultivar, Taiwan Tea Experiment Station number 18, released in 1999 by the station's Yuchi branch after decades of selection, and it is a cross between a large-leaf Assam line from Burma and Taiwan's own wild mountain tea. That parentage gives it something no other black tea has: a cooling mint-and-cinnamon note that Taiwanese drinkers call 'Taiwan fragrance'.

Black tea around Yuchi in Nantou dates from the Japanese period, when Assam seed was planted on the hills around the lake and a black tea research station was set up on Maolan Mountain in the 1930s. The industry collapsed in the export slump of the 1970s and 1980s and was rebuilt after the 1999 earthquake with Hong Yu as the star. The tea is made in the orthodox way, withered long, rolled into long twisted strips, fully oxidised and dried, with no cutting and no roast, and the leaf comes out as striking wiry black needles several centimetres long.

In the cup it is ruby-red, sweet and malty, with dark honey, a cinnamon warmth and that distinct mint-like coolness on the finish, and a hint of camphor in the best summer lots. It is smooth when brewed sensibly, water around 90 to 95 degrees and no more than three minutes Western-style, or short gongfu steeps in a pot big enough for the long leaf; boiling water and long steeps bring out tannin it does not need. It makes a superb cold brew and takes milk if you insist, though it is better without.

It is sold by harvest season and year. Summer leaf, picked from June to August, is prized for black tea here because the heat builds the aromatic compounds; spring lots are lighter and autumn sits between. The Yuchi Farmers' Association grades lots in its Sun Moon Lake black tea competition and the area has a certified-origin label worth looking for, since cheaper TTES number 8 is sometimes sold simply as 'Sun Moon Lake black'. Hong Yu is also grown in Hualien, Taitung and the Alishan foothills, and good lots come from all of them. It keeps two or three years sealed.

Try it against TTES number 21, Hong Yun, its citrus-scented younger sibling, or against number 8, the bold Assam that came before it.
sources_note: Parentage (Burmese Assam B-607 x Taiwan wild mountain tea B-729) and the 1999 release are from memory of TRES material. I did not find a dedicated English Wikipedia article I could name with confidence, so the umbrella article is used; 'Sun Moon Lake' (the lake) exists but is not about the tea.
